# Comparing LSTM and Transformer Models for Movie Review Sentiment Classification

## 1. Task and Research Question (2 points)

- Task: Binary text sequence classification. Given a movie review, predict whether its sentiment is positive or negative.
    
- Research question: How do an LSTM and a Transformer encoder compare when classifying movie review sentiment, and does review length affect their performance?
    
- Goal: Compare the models using standard classification metrics and examine examples where their predictions are incorrect.
    

## 2. Proposed Models (2 points)

- Model 1: LSTM classifier
    

- Convert review text into tokens and learned word embeddings.
    
- Process the variable-length token sequence with an LSTM layer.
    
- Pass the final hidden representation through a linear classification layer to predict positive or negative sentiment.
    

- Model 2: Transformer encoder classifier
    

- Convert tokens into embeddings and add positional encodings.
    
- Process the sequence using Transformer encoder layers with multi-head self-attention and feed-forward networks.
    
- Pool the sequence representations and use a linear layer for binary classification.
    

- Training and evaluation:
    

- Implement both models in PyTorch.
    
- Use binary cross-entropy with logits, an Adam optimizer, and validation data for selecting model settings.
    
- Compare accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrices.
    
- Analyze performance across short, medium, and long reviews.
    
- Begin with small experiments and verify that each model can overfit a single training example before full training.
    

  
  
  

## 3. Dataset and Data Exploration (4 points)

Dataset: [https://zenodo.org/records/7929635?preview_file=large_movie_review_dataset.zip](https://zenodo.org/records/7929635?preview_file=large_movie_review_dataset.zip) 

  

Size and labels:

- 50,000 labeled movie reviews.
    
- 25,000 training reviews and 25,000 test reviews.
    
- Binary labels: positive and negative, with balanced classes in the standard split.
    
- Reviews vary in length and contain natural-language expressions, negation, and differing writing styles.
    

- Access: The dataset is publicly accessible. We will verify and document the dataset card's license and usage terms before finalizing the proposal and cite the original dataset source.
    
- Planned exploration:
    

- Load the dataset and verify the number of examples and class distribution.
    
- Check for missing text, duplicate reviews, and unusually short or long reviews.
    
- Calculate minimum, median, and maximum review lengths and compare length distributions between classes.
    
- Inspect representative positive and negative reviews and plot the review-length distribution.
    
- Record observed findings and use them to select a reasonable maximum sequence length for model training.
    
- Preserve the official test split and create a validation split from the training data. Fit the vocabulary and preprocessing settings using training data only to prevent data leakage.
    

## 4. Ethical Considerations (2 points)

- Sentiment classification could help summarize large collections of reviews and analyze audience opinions.
    
- Potential harms: Incorrect predictions could misrepresent a reviewer's opinion, especially when the review expresses mixed feelings, sarcasm, or subtle criticism.
    
- Differences across groups: Models may interpret slang, dialects, non-native English, or culturally specific expressions differently, leading to uneven performance.
    
- The dataset reflects particular sources and time periods and may not represent all audiences, languages, or film cultures.
    
- We will examine misclassified examples, acknowledge dataset limitations, and avoid treating model predictions as definitive judgments of a person's opinion.
    

## 5. Division of Team Responsibilities (2 points)

Member 1 — Data preparation and baseline

- Download and document the dataset and its license.
    
- Inspect class balance, review lengths, missing values, and duplicates.
    
- Implement tokenization, data loading, and train/validation/test handling.
    
- Build a simple baseline classifier and produce dataset statistics and plots.
    

Member 2 — LSTM implementation

- Implement the embedding layer, LSTM, and binary classification head.
    
- Handle variable-length sequences and padding appropriately.
    
- Verify input and output dimensions and the loss calculation.
    
- Test overfitting on a single example, train the model, and record validation and test results.
    

Member 3 — Transformer implementation

- Implement token embeddings, positional encodings, Transformer encoder layers, pooling, and the classification head.
    
- Implement attention masks to handle padded tokens correctly.
    
- Verify the forward pass and overfit a single example.
    
- Train and evaluate the model and record validation and test results.
    

Member 4 — Experimental evaluation and error analysis

- Implement a shared evaluation pipeline for accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrices.
    
- Compare the LSTM and Transformer using the same test set and evaluation metrics.
    
- Analyze model performance across short, medium, and long reviews.
    
- Examine misclassified examples and identify potential reasons for incorrect predictions.
    
- Prepare comparison tables, visualizations, and the results section.
    

Shared responsibilities

- Agree on evaluation metrics, data splits, preprocessing methods, and experimental settings.
    
- Use validation data for model selection and reserve the official test set for final evaluation.
    
- Review misclassified examples, ethical considerations, and dataset limitations together.
    
- Integrate and test the code, document random seeds and model settings, and reproduce the main results.
    
- Compare model performance, training time, and computational costs.
    
- Collaborate on the final report, presentation, and discussion of findings.
    

  

## Reference

Maas, A. L., et al. (2011). Learning Word Vectors for Sentiment Analysis. Proceedings of ACL-HLT. IMDb Large Movie Review Dataset.

  
  
  

## 1. Most relevant papers

Read first

1. Chen and Lv (2022) — “Long Text Truncation Algorithm Based on Label Embedding in Text Classification”

Journal: Applied Sciences

This paper investigates how to shorten long documents for classification while trying to preserve useful information. It explicitly includes the IMDb movie-review dataset, making it a particularly relevant source for your project.

MDPI

Why it matters to you: It establishes that text truncation and its effect on classification performance have already been studied.

[Read the paper](https://doi.org/10.3390/app12199874?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

  
  
  
  

2. Tuteja and González Juclà (2023) — “Long Text Classification using Transformers with Paragraph Selection Strategies”

Conference: Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop, ACL

The authors evaluate ways of selecting text chunks for Transformer-based document classification. Their experiments explicitly compare strategies such as keeping the beginning, keeping the end, and keeping portions from both ends of long documents.

ACL Anthology

+1

Why it matters to you: This is one of the closest methodological matches to your proposed experiment. It means you should frame your contribution as a specific comparison on IMDb sentiment classification, rather than claiming that comparing beginning and ending text is a new idea.

[Read the paper and access the PDF](https://aclanthology.org/2023.nllp-1.3/?utm_source=chatgpt.com)
